title: How many primes can you make from the digits 2, 4 and 5?
description: The digits two, four and five are arranged in every order to make three digit numbers, and each number is tested for a factor besides one and itself. Every arrangement turns out composite.
teaching_notes: One idea: a multiple of two or of five has an extra factor, so a number made from the digits two, four and five cannot be prime. Watch for students who test only a few arrangements and miss that every ending is two, four or five.

video_script.why: The child lists all six arrangements and sees from the sieve that a multiple of two or of five is always crossed out.
video_script.substitution: Write every arrangement of the three digits and give each one a factor of two or five.
video_script.anchor: Three digit cards two, four and five that are arranged in every order
video_script.payoff_line: None of the six numbers is prime.
maths_rules: the arrangements of 2, 4, 5 are 245, 254, 425, 452, 524, 542 (6 of them, since 3 × 2 × 1 = 6)
every arrangement ends in 2, 4 or 5, so it is a multiple of 2 or of 5 and has a factor besides 1 and itself
video_script.design: Six arrangement cards are laid out; each gets a factor of two or five written beside it and turns amber.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; three digit cards 2, 4, 5 and three empty boxes

marks.cards: the three digit cards appear above three empty boxes
marks.ask: a question mark appears over the word prime

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about making numbers.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>Use each of the digits two, four and five once to make a three digit number.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many of these numbers can be prime?

beats.on_screen: the cards and boxes stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: multiples of 2 and 5 are crossed out in the table; a prime has exactly two factors

marks.cross: the multiples of two and five are crossed out in the table
marks.prime: a prime keeps only the factors one and itself

narration: <bookmark mark='cross'/>In the table, the later multiples of two and of five were all crossed out.
<bookmark mark='prime'/>A prime has only the factors one and itself, so a crossed out number is not prime.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the digits two, four and five, each used once.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many of the three digit numbers are prime

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many of the numbers are prime.

marks.list: the six arrangements are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step one, write every arrangement. There are six of them.
<bookmark mark='lower'/>They are two hundred and forty five, two hundred and fifty four, and four hundred and twenty five.
<bookmark mark='upper'/>Then come four hundred and fifty two, five hundred and twenty four, and five hundred and forty two.

marks.five: the two numbers ending in five get a factor of five
marks.two: the four numbers ending in two or four get a factor of two

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Step two, give each number a factor. Two hundred and forty five and four hundred and twenty five end in five, so five divides them.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The other four end in two or four, so they are even and two divides them.

beats.on_screen: Check: every arrangement ends in 2, 4 or 5, so none can escape

marks.end: the last digit of each of the six numbers is circled
marks.all: the six circles are matched with the digits two, four and five

narration: <bookmark mark='end'/>Step three, check the last digits. The last digit must be two, four or five, because those are the only digits we have.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Every arrangement is a multiple of two or of five, and none can escape.

beats.on_screen: Answer: None of the six numbers is prime
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>None of the six numbers is prime.
